item.title: Single quotes and double quotes have different expansion behavior
item.content: In Bash, single quotes preserve enclosed characters literally, while double quotes still allow parameter expansion and command substitution but prevent ordinary word splitting and pathname expansion of the quoted result.
item.explanationMarkdown:
Compare:

```bash
x=hello
printf '%s\n' '$x'
printf '%s\n' "$x"
```

The first prints `$x`; the second prints `hello`.

Double quotes are often the safe default around expansions such as `"$variable"` because the expanded value is kept as one argument (except for special constructs such as `"$@"`).

cards.question: In Bash, which statement about quoting is correct?
options: Single quotes allow variable expansion, while double quotes suppress it.
Both single and double quotes suppress all shell expansion.
Single quotes keep their contents literal, while double quotes still allow parameter expansion and command substitution.
Double quotes force pathname expansion but single quotes do not.
cards.explanation: Single quotes are literal. Double quotes still permit parameter expansion and command substitution while protecting the expanded text from ordinary splitting and globbing.
